# Arrays

Arrays generalize matrices to more than two dimensions.
```{r}
(aRray <- array(1:24, dim = c(3, 4, 2)))
class(aRray)
```

A classic use case is gridded (NetCDF-style) data: longitude as columns,
latitude as rows, and time as the third dimension — each time slice being
its own row x column matrix.
```{r}
dim(aRray)
aRray[1, 1, 2] # row 1, column 1, of the 2nd matrix "slice"
```

# Lists

A list holds objects of different types and sizes together.
```{r}
L <- list()
A <- matrix(0, 5, 6)

L$A <- A
L$my_seq <- sample(10, 5)
L$Bool <- TRUE
L[["iris_head"]] <- head(iris, 3)
length(L)

L[[5]] <- "I am learning R"
names(L)
names(L)[5] <- "String"
names(L)
```

```{r}
mylist <- list("matrix" = A,
               "sequence" = 1:5,
               "Bool" = TRUE)
mylist$matrix
class(mylist[[1]])
mylist[c("matrix", "Bool")]
```

# Data Frames

A data frame is a table of $n$ rows (observations) by $p$ columns
(variables), where each column can hold a different data type.

## Converting a continuous variable into categories
```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 120
df <- data.frame(
  "ID"  = paste0("Particip_", 1:n),
  "age" = sample(0:120, size = n)
)
head(df, 5)
```

```{r}
brks <- seq(0, 120, by = 10)
df$age_groups <- cut(df$age, breaks = brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
head(df, 5)
```

## Exercise: summarizing the age groups

1. Counts by age group:
```{r}
(counts <- table(df$age_groups))
```

2. A barplot of the age groups:
```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
x <- barplot(counts, col = "purple", main = "Distribution of ages", xaxt = "n")
text(x = x, y = -1.5, cex = 0.8, xpd = TRUE, srt = 45, labels = names(counts))
```

3. A histogram of raw ages:
```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
hist(df$age, main = "Histogram of ages", xlab = "age", col = "pink", breaks = 12)
```

4. IDs of participants in the (70, 80] age group:
```{r}
df$ID[df$age_groups == "(70,80]"]
```

```{r}
l <- split(df, df$age_groups)
names(l)
l$`(70,80]`$ID
```

## Creating a data frame directly
```{r}
df2 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10), y = rpois(10, 2))
head(df2, 3)
```
